Opening frame: What’s driving markets? Market take Camera frame Title slide: AI’s rising bill of expectations After two years of booming AI investment, we have seen more scrutiny on the AI theme as investors want to see the payoff. That shifting backdrop contributed to our decision to downgrade US equities to neutral last month. Our conviction in AI fundamentals, however, remains intact. 1: A different backdrop The backdrop for megacap tech looks very different from just a few months ago. Why? The earnings gap has now flipped for the first time since 2022 with the rest of the market expected to outpace the magnificent seven. AI leaders are still delivering, but their outperformance is becoming less exceptional. And with expectations already so high, investors are increasingly looking at whether monetization and cash generation can sustain investment. 2: Maintaining AI conviction Last week’s earnings highlighted a growing tension between strong demand for AI-linked goods and services and the rising cost of meeting it. Hyperscaler spending has surged, leaving little cash surplus after capex. Each additional dollar of revenue is generating less profit, raising questions about whether returns can keep pace with soaring investment. We do find early signs of AI adoption impacting earnings growth. Our analysis finds that companies outside big tech with higher AI adoption are on track for about 3% more earnings growth this quarter than those with lower adoption. Meanwhile rising cloud revenues also point to strong AI demand. 3: A broader view As the AI buildout is increasingly funded by debt, leverage and funding capacity are coming into sharp focus. The buildout is adding to competition for capital and keeping upward pressure on yields. We see the recent fall in yields as a reflection of the ebbs and flows of competition for capital as markets consider any emerging constraints on deploying even more funding. As such, credit markets are a key signpost of how much more AI investment can be financed — and at what cost. Outro: Here’s our Market take AI faces a tougher near-term test as investor scrutiny intensifies. But our conviction in AI fundamentals remains intact, keeping us selective on where we take AI exposure. Closing frame: Read details: blackrock.com/weekly-commentary AI under pressure Investor scrutiny of AI is intensifying this earnings season. How results hold up will be key to our broader medium-term conviction in the AI transformation. Market backdrop The Nasdaq posted its worst month since March 2025 as AI scrutiny intensified. We see multiple plausible outcomes for growth, profitability and returns. Week ahead We are watching October US jobs data amid signs of a tight labor market in recent months. Any further wage pressure could drive core services inflation. Four years of booming AI investment have sent earnings expectations soaring. Investors now want evidence that spending can deliver returns, especially as rising capital expenditures squeeze free cash flow, pushing it into negative territory for some firms. We recently downgraded US equities to neutral to lock in profits, but our core conviction in the AI transformation remains intact. That supports our EM equity overweight through exposure to bottlenecks in the AI buildout. Note: The bars show year-over-year earnings per share growth for the “magnificent seven” stocks (Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and Tesla) and the rest of S&P 500. Figures for Q3 and Q4 include estimates. We will learn much more about the AI theme this earnings season, especially how impactful the technology will ultimately be. But the backdrop for mega-cap tech stocks is starkly different from just four months ago. After narrowing considerably earlier this year, the earnings growth gap has now flipped for the first time since 2022, with the S&P 493 outpacing the “magnificent seven” at roughly 29% versus 18%. See the chart. The bar remains high. Consensus expects S&P 500 earnings to grow about 30% – marking a third consecutive quarter of growth above 20% – according to LSEG data. Meanwhile, scrutiny of the AI theme has grown. That shifting backdrop contributed to our decision to downgrade US equities to neutral last month. Our conviction in AI fundamentals, however, remains intact. Last week’s earnings highlighted a growing tension between strong demand for AI-linked goods and services and the rising cost of meeting it. Hyperscaler capital spending has surged to about $649 billion over the past year, from about $357 billion in the prior-year period, according to data from Bloomberg, leaving little cash surplus after capex. And while hyperscalers’ operating margins have edged up to 27.1% from 26.9% in the previous four quarters, incremental margins have fallen to 27.9% from 40.4% over that same period. In other words, each additional dollar of revenue is generating less additional profit, raising questions about whether returns can keep pace with soaring investment. Still, our analysis finds that companies with higher AI adoption outside the S&P 500 technology and communication sectors are on track for 3% higher earnings growth this quarter than lower adopters, based on evidence of AI use in regulatory filings. Cloud revenue growth at Microsoft and Alphabet also points to sustained momentum in AI demand. But whether that demand will be enough to justify the scale of investment is still an open question, one we plan to debate at our 2027 internal Outlook Forum this week. Funding capacity in focus As the AI buildout becomes increasingly debt-financed, leverage and differences in funding capacity are coming into sharper focus. Credit markets are becoming an important signpost of how much additional AI investment can be financed and at what cost. The Treasury rally alongside the tech sell-off this week also fits our view that the ebb and flow of AI investment expectations will drive competition for capital and bond yields around structurally higher levels. Within equities, we’re selective with our AI exposures. We favor companies and listed infrastructure poised to benefit from the critical bottlenecks in the AI buildout, a key reason for our move back to overweight EM equities in September. We see that opportunity playing out in Asia. Recent results from chipmakers point to tight supply and strong AI demand. But staying nimble is crucial, as our EM positioning shows: we upgraded at the start of the year, took profits midyear and returned to overweight in September. Brazil’s post-election selloff bears watching, but it does not change our EM overweight. Our bottom line AI faces a tougher near-term test as investor scrutiny intensifies. But our conviction in AI fundamentals remains intact, keeping us selective on where we take AI exposure while favoring opportunities tied to scarcity in the buildout. Market backdrop The Nasdaq Composite capped its worst month since March 2025 as concerns over returns on massive AI spending intensified. The key question now is the economic value of the AI buildout: what returns it generates and who captures them. We see a range of possible outcomes for growth, profitability and returns on this investment. US Treasuries extended their rally last week, with 10-year yields falling nearly 6 basis points to 4.93% after the Fed kept rates unchanged, as expected. We focus on October nonfarm payrolls for signs of a tightening labor market and what that could mean for inflation. We’d expect stronger wage pressures than in recent jobs reports, potentially adding to core services inflation, making the October jobs data key to assessing our view of price pressures. Intersecting mega forces Since we launched our mega forces framework it has become clearer how their intersection shapes almost all our investment views and opens up alpha opportunities. They cut across asset class labels, spurring a rethink of portfolio construction. Investors need to be deliberate about the economic or thematic exposures they own, the vehicles they use to implement them and their investment horizons. From drivers to portfolio expressions Our highest conviction views, November 2026 Driver What we think Portfolio expression Growth and AI scarcity AI fundamentals are strong, but we eye near-term volatility. Neutral US equities and overweight EM equities; favor AI- and tech-related opportunities. Duration and diversification Higher starting yields improve prospective returns and income. Overweight short-term US Treasuries for solid income and a cushion against higher rates; neutral long-term Treasuries Credit spreads and liquidity Selectivity is crucial amid tight spreads and uneven fundamentals. Credit with clear cash flows, lender protections and recovery value; higher-rated high yield. Inflation and scarcity Scarcity, secure supply and power demand carry inflation risks. Infrastructure, energy bottlenecks, EM local debt and real-asset-linked exposures. Alpha opportunity Macro outcomes matter again in the new regime. Asset class implications Six- to 12-month tactical positioning, November 2026 This shows the implementation of our key investment views from the previous page through an asset class lens. Search views Asset Tactical view Commentary Equities United States We are neutral. Strong AI fundamentals remain supportive, but policy uncertainty could fuel near-term volatility. We continue to favor AI and tech. Europe We are neutral. We would need to see more business-friendly policy and deeper capital markets for Europe to outperform. We favor financials, infrastructure, and industrials. UK We are neutral. Valuations remain attractive relative to the US, but we see few near-term catalysts to trigger a shift. Japan We are neutral. Strong corporate balance sheets and governance reforms remain supportive. We prefer targeted exposures to physical AI and the buildout’s bottlenecks. Emerging markets (EM) We are overweight. Strong earnings and cheaper valuations create opportunities. We particularly like different expressions of the AI scarcity theme across Asia and Latin America. China We are neutral. We see opportunities in physical AI. Cheap, open-source AI could drive adoption, but that doesn’t necessarily translate into AI-provider profitability. Fixed income Short US Treasuries We are overweight. Much of the repricing we anticipated has occurred, and expectations for further Fed hikes look excessive. We favor the front end for attractive income and a greater breakeven buffer. Long US Treasuries We are neutral. Higher yields offer attractive income and a bigger cushion against further rate increases. We still see room for yields to rise as competition for capital intensifies. Global inflation-linked bonds We are neutral. We see inflation settling above pre-pandemic levels, but markets may not price this in the near term as economic growth could slow. Euro area government bonds We are neutral short- and medium-term bonds. Current ECB rate pricing looks fairly valued given the balance of risks. Higher energy prices could push rates higher. We prefer to deploy risk elsewhere. UK Gilts We are neutral. We expect periods of elevated volatility given political uncertainty, longer-term bonds making up a larger market share, and buyers becoming more price-sensitive. Japanese government bonds We are underweight. The substantial repricing in yields has improved the risk-reward, but further rate hikes and heavy issuance could push yields higher. China government bonds We are neutral. China bonds offer stability and diversification but developed market yields are higher. A shift in investor sentiment toward equities limits upside. US agency MBS We are neutral and lean into the stable income MBS provide despite tight spreads. Short-term IG credit We are neutral. Spreads are tight due to corporate strength; they could widen if issuance increases or risk appetite shifts. Long-term IG credit We are underweight. We prefer short-term bonds less exposed to interest rate risk over long-term bonds. But attractive overall yields help offset the risk of increased issuance. Global high yield We are neutral. High yield offers attractive income. We prefer higher-rated US and European high yield over investment grade and see dispersion of returns increasing. Asia credit We are neutral. Overall yields are attractive and fundamentals are solid, but spreads are tight. Emerging hard currency We are neutral. Fundamentals have improved, but we see a more attractive risk-reward profile in EM local debt. Emerging local currency We are overweight. We like the yield relative to its volatility and improving fundamentals. Source Past performance is not a reliable indicator of current or future results. Euro-denominated tactical granular views Six to 12-month tactical views on selected assets vs. broad global asset classes by level of conviction, November 2026 We have lengthened our tactical investment horizon back to six to 12 months. The table below reflects this and, importantly, leaves aside the opportunity for alpha, or the potential to generate above-benchmark returns – especially at a time of heightened volatility. Search views Asset Tactical view Commentary Equities Europe ex UK We are neutral. We would need to see more business-friendly policy and deeper capital markets for Europe to outperform and to justify a broad overweight. We stay selective, favoring financials, infrastructure, industrials, materials and healthcare. Germany We are neutral. Higher spending on defense and infrastructure support the corporate sector. Valuations are not stretched but neither compelling and expected earnings growth lags other countries. Light positioning means potential easing in geopolitical tensions and AI lifting industrials-driven earnings could create opportunities. France We are neutral. Strong expected earnings growth and global revenue exposure support French corporates. Valuations are less compelling, albeit not stretched versus euro area peers. Persistent political uncertainty leaves the overall risk reward balanced. Italy We are neutral. Earnings growth and momentum are strong, boosted by the significant exposure to financials, utilities and energy. Valuations are still at discount vs. peers, but not as much as in previous years. Political risk is currently low but likely to pick up ahead of 2027 elections. Spain We are overweight. Valuations remain attractive vs. peers even if relative earnings momentum has slowed. Strong domestic demand growth and exposure to fast-growing areas like Latin America support Spanish stocks. Financials, utilities and infrastructure-linked stocks would benefit from Europe’s push towards autonomy. Netherlands We are neutral. Earnings revisions in the IT sector, a large sector in the Dutch stock market is offset by other sectors seeing less favorable valuations and a weaker earnings outlook than European peers. Switzerland We are neutral. Valuations have improved, from stretched levels, but the earnings outlook is weaker than other European markets. If global risk appetite stays strong, the index’s tilt to stable, less volatile sectors may weigh on performance. UK We are neutral. Valuations remain attractive relative to the US, but we see few near-term catalysts to trigger a shift. Fixed income Euro area government bonds We are neutral short- and medium-term bonds. Current ECB rate pricing looks fairly valued given the balance of risks. Higher energy prices could push rates higher. We prefer to deploy risk elsewhere. German bunds We are neutral Bunds. Current ECB rate pricing looks more fairly valued given the balance of risks. Fiscal stimulus and increased bond issuance exert upward pressure on yields, alongside inflation risks amid lingering geopolitical tensions. French OATs We are neutral. Elevated political uncertainty, high budget deficits and slow structural reforms could stoke volatility, but these risks already seem priced into OATs and we don’t expect a material worsening from here. Italian BTPs We are neutral. The spread over German bunds looks tight given Italy’s large budget deficits and growing public debt. Domestic factors remain supportive, with growth holding up relative to the rest of the euro area and local demand for BTPs solid at current yield levels. Domestic disapproval would likely prevent defense spending from reaching fiscally unstable levels. Political uncertainty is likely to increase ahead of next year’s elections. UK gilts We are neutral. We expect periods of elevated volatility given political uncertainty, longer-term bonds making up a larger market share, and buyers becoming more price-sensitive. Swiss government bonds We are neutral. The SNB seems comfortable with its medium-term inflation outlook and its current policy stance. Market pricing is broadly in line with SNB messaging. European inflation-protected securities We are neutral. We see higher medium-term inflation, but inflation expectations are firmly anchored. Cooling inflation and uncertain growth may matter more near term. European investment grade European investment grade is supported by healthy corporate sector balance sheets, contained default rates and the persistently strong demand for durable income from European households. We prefer European investment grade over the US. European high yield We are overweight. While spreads are low, the income potential remains attractive. Defaults are contained and high yield is of higher quality and less sensitive to interest rate swings compared with the US.
